# Interviewer Guide: Requirement Engine

## Source material

This question is grounded in a real Berkeleytime feature: **BtLL
(Berkeleytime Logical Language)**, documented at
`apps/docs/src/core/BtLL/README.md` in the main repo. BtLL is a whole custom
interpreted DSL: typed variables, user-defined functions, a `main` entry
point, and six specialized `Requirement` types (`BooleanRequirement`,
`NCoursesRequirement`, `CourseListRequirement`, `AndRequirement`,
`OrRequirement`, `NumberRequirement`) that compute a `result` field by
walking the program. Each degree/college/major's requirements were encoded as
a BtLL program and evaluated per-student.

The interesting part for this interview isn't the DSL syntax -- it's the
shipping history:

- `2d08ec826` -- **"Logic engine (#1030)"**, the original feature. Landed
  ~3000 lines of `reference_gradtrak_reqs.ts` (hand-encoded requirements for
  every major/college), a full interpreter package (`packages/BtLL`), and a
  895-line frontend interface component.
- `fa4890912` -- **"Revert 'Logic engine (#1030)'"**, later that same day
  (~15 hours after the original landed).
- `9971210e4` -- **"Logic engine v2 (#1123)"**, which is a revert-of-the-revert
  plus a lint fix -- i.e. the *same* implementation was shipped again the
  next day, essentially unchanged.

Run `git show --stat <sha>` on each of those three in the main repo if you
want the full file list. This is a great, low-effort conversation opener for
Round 1 or as a wrap-up question: **"This exact feature was shipped, reverted
later that same day, and reshipped essentially unchanged the next day. What
do you think went wrong, and why do you think the fix was 'ship it again'
rather than a redesign?"**
There's no single correct answer on record (the revert commit message gives
no reason) -- what you're listening for is whether the candidate can
generate plausible, specific failure modes for this *class* of system, not
whether they guess the real one. Good answers reach for things like:
performance on deeply nested trees evaluated per-student at page-load time,
an edge case in N-of-M counting when a course satisfies multiple leaves at
once (exactly the bug in this exercise's starter), a `.cursorrules` /
generated-code smell suggesting the whole thing may have been scaffolded
quickly, or the interpreter being unusable to *explain* results (all six
`Requirement` types compute a bare boolean `result`; there's no structured
"what's missing" output visible in the README at all -- see below).

Note also, as a design-judgment signal: BtLL is a full custom
language-with-an-interpreter for what is fundamentally a nested
boolean/counting evaluation problem over ~six data shapes. That's a lot of
machinery (parser, type system, function definitions, a `main` entrypoint)
for the actual complexity of the domain. Whether a candidate would build the
same thing, and whether they can say why or why not, is worth probing in
Round 1 (see Design 3 below).

---

## Round 1: System Design discussion guide

### The four designs

Use these as your rubric for whatever the candidate proposes -- they don't
need to land on one of these exactly, but a strong candidate's design should
be classifiable as one of these (or a hybrid) and they should be able to
articulate the tradeoff axis themselves.

| # | Design | Evaluation speed | Explainability | Complexity to build | Correctness under double-counting |
|---|--------|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Direct AST interpretation.** Parse/author into a tree of typed nodes (`AndNode`, `OrNode`, `NOfMNode`, `CourseLeafNode`); evaluate recursively per request against a student's course set. | Moderate -- re-walks the tree every time, but trees are small (dozens to low hundreds of nodes) and evaluation is O(tree size). | Best of the four -- the same recursive walk that computes `satisfied` can naturally also collect "why not" as it goes (this is what the starter code in this exercise does). | Low-moderate. | Depends entirely on the implementation -- this is exactly the case the Round 2 exercise's `n_of_m` contract is designed to probe. Nothing about "tree of nodes" forces you to get it right; you have to notice the edge case. |
| 2 | **Compile to a boolean circuit / CNF / decision diagram ahead of time**, evaluate the compiled form at request time. | Best -- compiled representation evaluates in near-constant/linear time over the (smaller) compiled form, good if evaluating millions of times. | Worst -- once flattened into CNF or a BDD, the original tree structure (which leaf, which branch) is gone or hard to recover; explaining "why" means either keeping a side-table back to the source tree (extra complexity) or not being able to explain at all. | High -- need a compiler step, a normalized IR, and (if you want explainability back) a mapping back to source. Harder to reason about while *authoring* requirements too, since you're not looking at the thing that runs. | Same underlying risk as #1 (N-of-M is a counting construct, not pure boolean logic -- doesn't fall out of CNF for free) but now the dedup logic has to survive being lowered into a different representation, which is an easy place to lose it. |
| 3 | **Generic rule engine** (off-the-shelf constraint solver, Prolog-like engine, or -- as BT actually built -- a whole custom DSL + interpreter). | Varies, often worse (general engines pay overhead the specific domain doesn't need). | Can be good (many rule engines have built-in explanation/trace facilities) but only if you build/use that part -- BtLL's README shows no such facility; every `Requirement` type just computes a boolean `result`. | Highest. This is real, shipped evidence of the cost: a parser, a type system, ~15 built-in function categories, a whole interpreter package, docs, and an authoring UI, to encode what is fundamentally 4-5 node types over course data. Worth naming explicitly as a probable **over-engineering** case study. | No inherent advantage -- still requires the implementer to think about it. |
| 4 | **Precomputed satisfaction bitmask per requirement per student**, recomputed on course-plan change. | Best for reads (dashboard just reads a stored bit), worst for writes (every course-plan edit must trigger recompute of every affected requirement). | Poor by default -- a bitmask is exactly a boolean, nothing more; you'd need to store/recompute an explanation payload alongside it, doubling the staleness-management problem. | Moderate-high -- need a recompute trigger (on every plan edit, catalog change, tag change...) and a staleness/invalidation story. Good for a "GradTrak dashboard shows N students' status at once" read pattern; bad if the tree changes often (catalog year changes, requirement edits). | Whatever bug exists in the recompute function now exists in a value that's silently stale until the next trigger fires -- an extra failure mode on top of getting the logic right. |

There is no single "correct" choice among these -- for a course-planning tool
serving one student's audit page at a time, on read, #1 is the obviously
right starting point (and is the shape the starter's `RequirementNode` types
already assume, though the candidate writes the evaluator itself). The
interview signal is in whether the candidate can name the *actual* tradeoff
(explainability vs. raw throughput vs. build cost vs. correctness risk) for
whichever one they pick, and whether they'd revisit the choice under
different assumptions (e.g. "what if this had to serve 50,000 students'
dashboards refreshing every few seconds" should visibly push them toward
something like #4, with them proactively flagging the staleness cost).

### Follow-up questions to ask

- "Walk me through evaluating your data structure for example 2 (the CS
  major with a track requirement nested inside an OR) by hand, for a student
  who has 61A/61B/70/61C and none of the electives. What does your evaluator
  return, and what does the UI show them?"
- "A course satisfies two different leaves in the tree at once -- say, a
  specific-course requirement and a separate tag-based requirement in an
  unrelated branch. Should completing it count toward both? What does your
  design do about that today, on its own, without you special-casing it?"
- Now the harder version: "What if the same course satisfies two leaves
  *inside the same N-of-M node* -- e.g. one course carries two of the three
  tags an N-of-M(2 of 3) is checking? Does your design count that as 1
  distinct course or as 2 of the N? Which should it be, and why?" (This is
  exactly the distinction the Round 2 starter's `n_of_m` contract turns on --
  if the candidate reasons their way to "it should require 2 distinct
  courses, not 2 satisfied leaves" here, they are well set up for Round 2.)
- "How would your explanation ('what's missing') logic handle an OR where
  one branch already passed? Would it accidentally tell the student they're
  also missing courses from the losing branch?"
- "If this had to run once per page load for one student, vs. compute a
  status for 10,000 students on some schedule, does your design change?"

### Red flags

- **Can't represent N-of-M at all** -- only reaches for pure AND/OR and has
  to hand-wave "3 of these 5 electives" as, e.g., an OR of every
  `C(5,3)`-combination (a real but very wrong instinct -- ask them to
  compute how many branches that is for "5 of 10").
- **No consideration of explainability** until directly prompted by question
  3 in README.md -- treats this as pure boolean SAT with no notion of "how
  close is this student," and once prompted, cannot describe *how* their
  chosen data structure would produce an explanation (vs. just asserting "we
  could add that").
- **Never notices the double-counting question is a question** -- assumes
  without examination that of course a course can satisfy multiple leaves,
  or of course it can't, without being able to say what breaks if they're
  wrong, or that the answer might differ between "different branches" and
  "same N-of-M node."
- Jumps straight to a generic rule engine / solver / DSL (Design 3) as the
  obvious answer without weighing it against 1/2/4 -- fine if they can
  defend it, a red flag if they can't articulate why the added machinery is
  worth it here.

## Round 2: Code review guide

### What the starter's tests check

Both `evaluateRequirement` and `getMissingLeaves` are fully stubbed (each
just throws `"not implemented"`), so on a fresh checkout all 17 tests in
`impl/test/evaluate.test.ts` fail identically -- there's no partial-credit
signal from the test run itself (previously, before this kit was reworked,
one function was pre-implemented with a bug and the split was 9 pass / 8
fail; now it's 0/17 until the candidate has written real logic for both
functions). What each test verifies about a CORRECT implementation:

- **Basic AND** over a flat set of tag leaves (the breadth-requirement
  fixture) -- sanity check before anything nested.
- **Nested AND/OR/N-of-M, 3+ levels deep** (the CS-major fixture: AND at the
  top, an OR for lab equivalency, an N-of-M for electives, and an OR-of-ANDs
  for the track requirement) -- both a fully-satisfied and a partially
  -satisfied student.
- **N-of-M counting**, correct in the basic case (distinct courses covering
  distinct tags).
- **Double counting, both directions**:
  - *Allowed*: the same course satisfying two different leaves in two
    different AND branches (and, separately, the realistic case embedded in
    the CS-major fixture where COMPSCI 162 is legitimately both one of the
    electives and half of the Systems Track).
  - *Not allowed*: one physical course carrying two of the three tags
    checked by a single N-of-M(2 of 3) node must NOT count as 2 distinct
    courses. A correct `n_of_m` case counts DISTINCT backing courses, not
    the count of satisfied children -- getting this wrong (counting
    satisfied children instead) is the single most common mistake this
    exercise is designed to surface.
- **`getMissingLeaves` (explainability)**: empty for a fully satisfied tree,
  exactly the one missing leaf in an otherwise-complete flat requirement,
  that already-satisfied children (and their leaves) are never reported as
  missing, that both options of an unsatisfied OR are reported, that a
  human-readable ancestor path is attached to each missing leaf, and the
  subtle case where an individual leaf is satisfied on its own but its
  parent N-of-M still isn't (because it shares a course with a sibling
  leaf) -- that leaf must NOT show up as "missing."

### Reference solution sketch

One correct approach to `evaluateRequirement`:

```ts
function courseIdsSatisfyingLeaf(leaf: LeafNode, student: Student): string[] {
  if (leaf.type === "course") {
    return student.completedCourses.some((c) => c.courseId === leaf.courseId)
      ? [leaf.courseId]
      : [];
  }
  return student.completedCourses
    .filter((c) => c.tags.includes(leaf.tag))
    .map((c) => c.courseId);
}

function evaluateRequirement(node: RequirementNode, student: Student): EvaluationResult {
  switch (node.type) {
    case "course":
    case "tag": {
      const satisfiedBy = courseIdsSatisfyingLeaf(node, student);
      return { node, satisfied: satisfiedBy.length > 0, satisfiedBy };
    }
    case "and": {
      const children = node.children.map((c) => evaluateRequirement(c, student));
      return { node, satisfied: children.every((c) => c.satisfied), children };
    }
    case "or": {
      const children = node.children.map((c) => evaluateRequirement(c, student));
      return { node, satisfied: children.some((c) => c.satisfied), children };
    }
    case "n_of_m": {
      // Count DISTINCT backing units, not satisfied children.
      const children = node.children.map((c) => evaluateRequirement(c, student));
      const usedUnits = new Set<string>();
      children.forEach((child, i) => {
        if (!child.satisfied) return;
        if (child.satisfiedBy?.length) {
          child.satisfiedBy.forEach((cid) => usedUnits.add(cid));
        } else {
          usedUnits.add(`__child_${i}`); // composite child: its own unit
        }
      });
      return { node, satisfied: usedUnits.size >= node.n, children };
    }
  }
}
```

One correct approach to `getMissingLeaves` -- only recurse into children
that are themselves unsatisfied:

```ts
function getMissingLeaves(result: EvaluationResult, prefix = ""): MissingLeaf[] {
  if (result.satisfied) return [];
  if (result.node.type === "course" || result.node.type === "tag") {
    return [{ leaf: result.node, path: pathFor(result.node, prefix) }];
  }
  const here = pathFor(result.node, prefix);
  return (result.children ?? [])
    .filter((c) => !c.satisfied)
    .flatMap((c) => getMissingLeaves(c, here));
}
```

The `usedUnits.add(\`__child_${i}\`)` fallback (for a composite child of an
N-of-M with no `satisfiedBy` of its own) is a stretch case the starter's
fixtures don't force -- a strong candidate may raise it unprompted ("what if
one of the N-of-M's children isn't a leaf?"); that's worth calling out as
good instinct even though the provided tests don't require handling it.

### Questions on AI tool usage

- "Which parts did you have AI generate vs. write yourself? Walk me through
  a prompt you used for `evaluateRequirement`."
- "Did AI's first draft of `evaluateRequirement` handle the N-of-M
  double-counting distinction correctly on its own, or did you have to steer
  it there? What tipped you off if it was wrong?"
- "Did the AI's first attempt at `getMissingLeaves` get the OR-with-a-passing-
  branch case right on its own, or did you have to correct it? How did you
  notice if it was wrong?"
- "Did you ask it to explain the double-counting distinction (allowed across
  branches, not allowed within one N-of-M), or did you have to supply that
  reasoning yourself?"

### Red flags

- Evaluator works on the simple/flat fixture but breaks on the 3-level-deep
  CS-major tree -- suggests they didn't actually generalize the recursion,
  just pattern-matched the shallow case.
- Implements N-of-M dedup in a way that also breaks the "double counting is
  fine across branches" case (i.e., they build some global "used courses"
  pool that gets consumed as the whole tree evaluates, rather than scoping
  the dedup to within a single N-of-M node). This is the single most
  diagnostic mistake to watch for -- it means they solved the letter of the
  failing test without understanding *why* the dedup has to be scoped where
  it is.
- Cannot explain their own recursion when asked to trace it by hand through
  the CS-major/partial-student case at the whiteboard -- particularly, can't
  say why an already-satisfied electives course (161) shouldn't show up as
  "missing" even though the electives N-of-M node overall is unsatisfied.
- Silently changes the shape of `RequirementNode`, `EvaluationResult`, or
  `MissingLeaf` to dodge a hard case instead of implementing the harder
  logic (e.g. adding a `satisfied: boolean` shortcut field that bypasses
  `satisfiedBy`-based dedup).
- Can't articulate the difference between "why is this false" (a boolean
  fact) and "what specifically should the student do next" (an action) when
  asked to compare their `getMissingLeaves` output to a hypothetical UI
  string.

---

## Rubric (1-5 each)

| Dimension | 1 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **System design judgment** | Can't represent N-of-M or nesting at all | Represents the tree correctly; picks one design without comparing tradeoffs | Correctly identifies where design choice matters (speed vs. explainability vs. build cost) and adapts the choice to stated constraints |
| **Code quality / correctness** | Evaluator breaks on nested/N-of-M cases even after the interview | Gets N-of-M dedup right but explanation logic is incomplete or over-reports | All tests pass; recursion is generalized, not hard-coded to the fixtures; can trace it by hand |
| **Tradeoff articulation** | States a design with no reasoning about cost | Names one tradeoff axis when prompted | Proactively surfaces multiple axes (explainability, scale, staleness, correctness risk) unprompted |
| **AI-tool usage judgment** | Can't describe what came from AI vs. them, or blindly accepted broken output | Used AI productively but needed prompting to explain review process | Clear account of what was generated, what was checked/corrected, and why -- treats AI output as a draft to verify, not an answer |
| **Communication** | Can't explain their own recursion or design when asked to trace an example | Explains when asked, with some back-and-forth needed | Proactively walks through concrete examples unprompted, at whatever altitude the interviewer needs |

---

## Time budget

| Segment | Time |
|---|---|
| Round 1: problem framing + candidate design | 10 min framing, 35-50 min design + discussion |
| Round 1: wrap-up ("what went wrong the first time?") | 5 min |
| Round 2: setup + task framing | 10 min |
| Round 2: implementation | 3-3.5 hours |
| Round 2: code review + AI-usage discussion | 30-45 min |
